newsitem.title: TANZANIA: U.N. Rwanda trial hears first expert witness.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Rwanda trial hears first expert witness.

text.p: A doctor with an aid agency on Thursday told the United Nations Rwanda war crimes tribunal that he saw hundreds of corpses and scores of Tutsis being killed in a series of incidents.

The court -- which was hearing from its first expert witness -- also ruled that former mayor of Rwanda's Taba commune Jean-Paul Akayesu, who is accused of genocide, could no longer cross-examine witnesses.
Rony Zachariah, a doctor with aid agency Medicins Sans Frontieres (Doctors Without Borders, MSF) based in Butare in April 1994, said in his testimony:
"We could see piles of bodies in fact the entire landscape was becoming spotted with corpses," Zachariah said of a journey to the Burundian border to collect medical supplies.

"There was another group of militia waiting and all these civilians between 60 to 80 were pursued and hacked to death...I presumed that they were Tutsis," he said of an incident on the Burundian border, adding that around 10 survived.
The court saw Zachariah's slides of corpses piled in fields and bodies chopped up and floating down the Kagera river on the Rwanda-Burundi border.
Zachariah said he closed his mission and evacuated his team on April 24 after Tutsi nurses and patients were taken from the hospital and killed.

"What we seek to prove is that in Rwanda there was a widespread and systematic attack against the civilian population and Akayesu's acts were part of that global crime," prosecutor Yacob Haile-Mariam told the court.
Zachariah's evidence is critical to the prosecution, which must prove Akayesu participated in a genocide rather than in isolated killings. Zachariah did not mention Akayesu in his testimony.

Akayesu, 43, is accused of genocide and crimes against humanity in the 1994 mass killings of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus sparked off by the assassination of Hutu president and military strongman Juvenal Habyarimana.
Angry Habyarimana followers took up arms and hunted down Tutsis and moderate Hutus opposed to his junta.
Zachariah said the decision to testify before the tribunal was taken after an intense debate within MSF which finally decided Rwanda needed justice more than bandages.

Earlier presiding Judge Laity Kama decided that Akayesu could no longer cross-examine witnesses directly. Kama gave the ruling as part of a decision to prevent Akayesu from dismissing his two lawyers after he twice fired previous counsel.
"The decision has been taken that you (Akayesu) can no longer cross-examine witnesses except through your counsel...This is the decision of the court," Kama said.
Akayesu cross-examined three prosecution witnesses during the trial's first week sparking clashes between victim and accused.

The witnesses claimed Akayesu ordered killings of Tutsis at Taba commune. Two witnesses, a Hutu farmer and a 70-year-old Hutu woman, told the court Akayesu beat and tortured them in an attempt to find out the whereabouts of a Tutsi woman he wanted.
Akayesu has pleaded not guilty to genocide and crimes against humanity during the mass killings.
Akayesu is the first suspect to be tried before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, set up in November 1994 to bring to justice the central figures in the genocide.
A total of 21 people have been indicted by the tribunal, of whom seven are in custody at the tribunal headquarters in northern Tanzania.
Kama said the court would adjourn until Friday.
Rwanda holds 90,000 people suspected of taking part in the genocide but has only just started putting them on trial. Two Hutu men were sentenced to death in Rwanda on January 3.
